info.text: Interactive check questions for Lesson 13.2: The TEI Processing Model, ODD, and TEI Publisher Transformation Pipelines.

name.text: 01 Question: The Evolution of TEI Publication: From Ad-Hoc XSLT to Declarative Models

questiontext.text: Why did legacy digital editing projects suffer from relying on bespoke, monolithic XSLT stylesheets?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI Processing Model replaces brittle, custom XSLT stylesheets with standardized, declarative rendering rules embedded directly in the schema.

answer.text: Custom XSLT stylesheets were brittle black boxes that tightly coupled presentation to idiosyncratic code, preventing reuse across projects.

feedback.text: Correct. Hand-crafted XSLT mixed parsing, XPath queries, and hard-coded HTML, breaking whenever schemas evolved or formats changed.

answer.text: XSLT was incapable of transforming XML documents into HTML or PDF formats.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XSLT is Turing-complete and capable of transformation, but custom monolithic stylesheets create severe maintenance debt.

answer.text: XSLT was declared illegal by international copyright organizations.

feedback.text: Incorrect. XSLT is a standard W3C technology; the issue was architectural brittleness and lack of interoperability.

answer.text: TEI XML files cannot be read by XML transformation processors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. TEI XML is fully standard XML, but bespoke stylesheets could not be shared or maintained easily.

name.text: 02 Question: The Myth of Presentation in Digital Humanities

questiontext.text: What is the 'Myth of Presentation' identified by Turska, Cummings, and Rahtz?

generalfeedback.text: Visual presentation is an integral dimension of scholarly communication that must be formalized declaratively within the edition's schema.

answer.text: The false belief that textual encoding is entirely detached from visual rendering and that presentation can be treated as an arbitrary afterthought.

feedback.text: Correct. Editorial markup implies explicit visual reading behaviors; the Processing Model formalizes presentation as a first-class scholarly dimension.

answer.text: The idea that digital editions should never use images or colors.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The myth refers to the false separation of encoding semantics from rendering intent, not a rejection of graphics.

answer.text: The belief that printed books will completely disappear within five years.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The myth concerns the theoretical relationship between XML markup and visual presentation.

answer.text: The assumption that ancient scribes never cared about page layouts.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Historical scribes cared deeply about layout; the myth concerns modern digital humanities theory.

name.text: 03 Question: The ODD (One Document Does It All) Philosophy: Unified Specification

questiontext.text: How does the ODD format solve the problem of documentation, schema, and stylesheets drifting apart?

generalfeedback.text: An ODD file serves as the single source of truth, generating human-readable guidelines, validation schemas, and publication transformations from one file.

answer.text: It unifies human-readable prose guidelines, formal validation schemas, and output processing models in a single XML master file.

feedback.text: Correct. Compiling an ODD file automatically generates Relax NG schemas, Schematron rules, and publication stylesheets from one source.

answer.text: It replaces XML schemas with unformatted plain-text readme files.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ODD generates rigorous Relax NG and Schematron schemas directly from structured XML declarations.

answer.text: It enforces that all digital editions must be written in a single non-standard programming language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ODD is standard TEI XML that compiles into standard web and schema languages.

answer.text: It eliminates the need for prose guidelines in digital editing projects.

feedback.text: Incorrect. ODD integrates prose documentation directly with schema specifications.

name.text: 04 Question: TEI P5 Chapter 22: The Architecture of the TEI Processing Model

questiontext.text: What core architectural insight underpins the TEI Processing Model in Chapter 22 of the Guidelines?

generalfeedback.text: The TEI Processing Model maps hundreds of diverse TEI elements onto a compact set of abstract, platform-agnostic rendering behaviors.

answer.text: Hundreds of diverse TEI elements can be mapped onto a compact set of abstract, platform-agnostic rendering behaviors.

feedback.text: Correct. Instead of writing custom HTML/LaTeX for every tag, elements invoke abstract behaviors (inline, block, note, alternate) that engines adapt to any medium.

answer.text: Every TEI tag must be assigned its own unique, custom programming language.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model unifies hundreds of elements through a standardized set of predefined behaviors.

answer.text: All digital editions must be compiled strictly into unstyled plain text.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The Processing Model supports rich, multi-modal web, print, and PDF presentation.

answer.text: Only five TEI elements are permitted in scholarly critical editions.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The model accommodates the full TEI vocabulary by mapping elements onto abstract behaviors.

name.text: 10 Question: Context-Sensitive Styling: The predicate XPath Condition

questiontext.text: How does the transformation engine determine which `` rule to execute when an element has multiple models?

generalfeedback.text: The `@predicate` attribute evaluates XPath expressions to apply context-sensitive rendering rules based on attributes, ancestors, and active modes.

answer.text: It evaluates `@predicate` XPath expressions sequentially and executes the first model whose predicate evaluates to true.

feedback.text: Correct. Sequential evaluation allows specific contextual rules (e.g., `@rend='rubric'`) to take precedence over generic fallback models.

answer.text: It executes all models simultaneously, merging their outputs into a single jumbled tag.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The engine executes only the first matching model rule.

feedback.text: Incorrect. Evaluation is strictly deterministic based on document order and XPath predicates.

answer.text: It executes the last model in the file, ignoring all earlier rules.

feedback.text: Incorrect. The engine stops at the first matching predicate; fallback models are placed last.
